verses.text: Two whole years later, Pharaoh had a dream. He was standing beside the River Nile,
when out of the river came seven cows, healthy and fat, and they ate the grass among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows came up out of the Nile, ugly and thin. They stood beside the other cows on the bank of the river.
Then the ugly, thin cows ate up the seven healthy, fat cows. And Pharaoh woke up.
He fell asleep again and had a second dream. Seven heads of grain, full and good, were growing on one stalk.
After them, seven other heads of grain sprouted. They were thin and dried up by the hot east wind.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven full, healthy heads. Then Pharaoh woke up, and he realised it had been a dream.
In the morning he was worried, so he sent for all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could tell him what they meant.
Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, "Today I am reminded of my failures.
Pharaoh was once angry with his servants, and he put me and the chief baker in custody in the house of the captain of the guard.
One night each of us had a dream, and each dream had its own meaning.
A young Hebrew man was there with us. He was a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he explained them to us. He told each of us what our dream meant.
And things turned out exactly as he said they would. I was given back my job, and the baker was hanged."
So Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and he was quickly brought out of the dungeon. When he had shaved and changed his clothes, he came to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I had a dream, and no one can tell me what it means. But I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream, you can explain it."
"I cannot do it," Joseph replied to Pharaoh, "but God will give Pharaoh the answer he needs."
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile,
when out of the river came seven cows, fat and healthy, and they ate the grass among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows came up. They were weak, very ugly and thin. I have never seen such ugly cows in all the land of Egypt.
The thin, ugly cows ate up the seven fat cows that came up first.
But even after they had eaten them, no one could tell that they had done so. They still looked just as ugly as before. Then I woke up.
In my dream I also saw seven heads of grain, full and good, growing on one stalk.
After them, seven other heads sprouted, withered and thin and dried up by the east wind.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven good heads. I told this to the magicians, but none of them could explain it to me."
Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, "The two dreams of Pharaoh mean the same thing. God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good heads of grain are seven years. It is one and the same dream.
The seven thin, ugly cows that came up afterwards are seven years, and so are the seven worthless heads of grain dried up by the east wind. They are seven years of famine.
It is just as I said to Pharaoh. God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do.
Seven years of great plenty are coming throughout the land of Egypt.
But after them, seven years of famine will follow. Then all the plenty in Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will ruin the land.
The good years will not be remembered, because the famine that follows will be so terrible.
The dream was given to Pharaoh in two forms because God has firmly decided this, and God will do it soon.
So now Pharaoh should look for a wise man with good understanding and put him in charge of the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh should appoint officials over the land to collect a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of plenty.
They should collect all the food of these good years that are coming and store up the grain under the authority of Pharaoh. It should be kept in the cities for food.
This food will be held in reserve for the country, to be used during the seven years of famine that will come on Egypt. Then the country will not be ruined by the famine."
The plan seemed good to Pharaoh and to all his officials.
So Pharaoh asked them, "Can we find anyone like this man, who has the Spirit of God in him?"
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has shown you all this, there is no one as wise and understanding as you.
You will be in charge of my palace, and all my people will obey your orders. Only I, because I sit on the throne, will be greater than you."
So Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I now put you in charge of the whole land of Egypt."
Then Pharaoh took his signet ring from his finger and put it on Joseph's finger. He dressed him in robes of fine linen and put a gold chain around his neck.
He had him ride in a chariot as his second-in-command, and people shouted in front of him, "Make way!" So Pharaoh put him in charge of the whole land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, but without your permission no one will lift a hand or foot in all Egypt."
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-Paneah. He also gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife. And Joseph travelled throughout the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he began serving Pharaoh king of Egypt. He went out from Pharaoh's presence and travelled all over Egypt.
During the seven years of plenty, the land produced huge harvests.
Joseph collected all the food produced in Egypt during those seven years and stored it in the cities. In each city he stored the food grown in the fields around it.
Joseph stored up huge amounts of grain, like the sand of the sea. There was so much that he stopped keeping records, because it was more than could be measured.
Before the years of famine came, Joseph had two sons by Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
Joseph named his firstborn Manasseh, which sounds like "forget", because he said, "God has made me forget all my trouble and all my father's family."
He named the second son Ephraim, which sounds like "fruitful", because he said, "God has made me fruitful in the land where I have suffered."
The seven years of plenty in Egypt came to an end,
and the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all the other lands, but in the whole land of Egypt there was food.
When all Egypt began to feel the famine, the people cried out to Pharaoh for food. Then Pharaoh told all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph and do what he tells you."
When the famine had spread over the whole country, Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians, because the famine was terrible throughout Egypt.
And people from all over the world came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine was terrible everywhere.
